frozen_acceptance.scope: A conservative descriptive quality/efficiency screen for this bounded run, not statistical significance or automatic deployment permission.
frozen_acceptance.quality: Require non-negative ON-minus-OFF weighted quality mean and no ON critical error in each split; report per-question regressions even if means pass.
frozen_acceptance.strict_evidence: Require no decrease in strict full-fact macro recall or all-facts-full questions in either split, and a positive full-fact gain on new_document_holdout. Partial evidence is not a substitute.
frozen_acceptance.source_noise: Require no increase in wholly irrelevant-label macro rate in either split; also report micro counts and denominator changes.
frozen_acceptance.runtime_tokens: Require no added answer-pipeline provider calls and no increase in mean prompt or total provider tokens in either split; disclose every individual increase.
frozen_acceptance.interpretation: Failing any screen prevents a claim of a reliable no-extra-token quality improvement. Passing only nominates further validation; two held-out papers and four questions do not justify universal claims or default activation.

decisions.reason: No entire source is irrelevant under the requested conservative rule. S1 directly describes question/title/passage input, independent encoding, concatenated representations, decoder-only fusion, and linear passage-count computation. S2 and S3 connect multi-passage aggregation and larger retrieved-passage sets with the method's reported behavior. Although S4 is mainly a benchmark table, its final passage begins the method's retrieval description and explicitly identifies BM25, so it contains relevant input-pipeline material. S5 is mostly dataset details, but includes the Figure 3 caption explicitly identifying FiD performance as a function of retrieved-passage count, which is relevant to the requested scaling discussion. S6 directly connects passage count with performance and training-computation costs, including a fewer-passages training tradeoff. S7 describes the retrieval-then-generation pipeline and scaling to one hundred passages. S8 is related work rather than evidence that FiD itself was trained end-to-end, but it explicitly attributes weakly supervised or end-to-end retrieval training to other named work; retain it as attribution/caveat context for the question about whether this paper implemented joint learning, without treating it as support for an affirmative FiD implementation claim.

S1 concerns the post-submission Transformers port, released scripts/demo, and index compression reducing CPU memory to 36GB; it does not discuss training supervision, the optimization objective, which parameters are updated, or periodic index rebuilding. S7 concerns human-evaluation annotators and implementation logistics (Fairseq, arithmetic precision, GPUs, CPU search, and index storage memory); none of those passages identifies the joint-training update boundary, supervision, objective, or the cost/necessity of refreshing the index. Index storage footprint alone does not establish the requested index-update explanation. Preserve the mixed or qualifying sources: S2 distinguishes index hot-swapping without retraining and future joint pretraining from the reported method; S3 gives question-answer supervision, answer likelihood, and document-index construction; S4 identifies the retriever/generator components; S5 explicitly says the authors do not train the document encoder; S6 supplies the important caveat that DPR initialization had retrieval supervision; and S8 directly describes freezing versus learning the retriever during training.

No excerpt is wholly irrelevant. S1 directly states the same-model, same-token-budget instruction overhead, simultaneous document-capacity tradeoff, reported accuracy ordering, and truncation procedure. S2 supplies concrete preprompt token overhead. S3 explains token-limit warnings and pagination, relevant to why memory management does not enlarge the simultaneous context window. S4 supplies the finite-window versus long-document limitation. S5 explicitly connects truncation with performance degradation in the reported comparisons. S7 distinguishes repeated archival retrieval and effective document access from documents simultaneously fitting in context. S8 makes the same finite-window versus iterative memory-access distinction. S6 is mainly broad conclusions and future work, but retains relevant fixed-context hierarchical-memory framing and the concrete GPT-4/function-calling implementation caveat; it is therefore not an entirely irrelevant source.

S4 concerns conversation-opener engagement, CSIM, and persona/recall ablations, not document capacity, document-QA accuracy, or document truncation. S5 reports conversational persona/summary/recall comparisons and DMR performance; its discussion of lossy conversation summaries does not address the requested retrieved-document truncation experiment. S7 concerns nesting-depth failures and multi-hop key-value lookup, not the document-count/token-budget tradeoff or truncation cost. S8 defines conversational consistency and engagement criteria, with no evidence about the requested document-QA comparison. Retain S1, which directly supplies all three requested topics; S2, which establishes the specific document-QA evaluation and common retriever; S3, which distinguishes repeated archival access from simultaneous context capacity and supplies retrieval limitations; and S6, which explicitly links main-memory capacity to context length and is useful context for the fixed-budget condition.

Legacy missing setup measurements stay null.

Its paired mean describes cold-start-equivalent cost, not total run expenditure: never sum upfront_setup_latency_ms across answers. corpus_ingestion retains each corpus once; setup is local work with real elapsed cost, not free provider tokens.
